opus-5.5.text:
I think the pressure is very real, and it comes from a few places at once.

First, the field is moving incredibly fast. In robotics especially, the last few years changed everything. We went from hand-engineering controllers for each task to training large models that can generalize across tasks and embodiments. When the paradigm shifts like that, everyone feels there is a window, maybe a couple of years, where whoever figures out the right recipe first gets a huge advantage. That window creates a sense of urgency, and urgency easily turns into long hours.

Second, there's a lot of capital flowing in. Humanoid and embodied AI startups are raising big rounds, and investors expect fast progress, demos, milestones. When your runway depends on showing the next impressive video, teams push very hard. On the big-lab side, there's competition between companies and also between the US and China, so nobody wants to be the one who falls behind.

Third, and specific to robotics, the work is physical. In pure AI you can launch a training job and go home. In robotics someone has to be there: collecting data, fixing hardware, resetting the scene, debugging why the gripper broke again. The physical world doesn't scale like compute, so people end up filling the gap with their own time.

But my personal view is that long hours are not the same as progress. The biggest breakthroughs I've seen came from having the right insight, picking the right problem, and not wasting effort on the wrong direction. A tired team makes worse decisions. Research is a marathon, even if it currently feels like a sprint. So what I try to do with my team is be very intense about focus and prioritization, cut what doesn't matter, and protect time for people to think. Sometimes there are crunch periods, before a deadline or a big launch, and that's fine. But as a permanent culture, I think 996 burns people out, and in a field this long-term, the people who stay healthy and curious for ten years will contribute much more than those who burn out in two.

r001.rationale: The response describes fear of falling behind, but does not say that top team members would leave for a leading team.

r002.rationale: It cites competition, investor expectations, and urgency as causes of long hours, but does not connect intensified work to retaining talent.

r003.rationale: The response says rapid progress creates urgency; it does not attribute recent progress partly to research effort induced by competition.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as the podcast guest, Jie Tan, drawing only on the conversation so far.

Honestly, I think the pressure is real, but people often misread where it comes from. In AI and robotics right now, the field moves so fast that a result you have today can be scooped or made irrelevant in six months. So the fear isn't really "my boss wants me at the office." It's "if I don't move now, the window closes." That fear sits on founders and researchers alike, and it gets translated downward into long hours.

A second piece is capital. Robotics companies especially are burning money on hardware, data collection, and compute, and the runway is short. Investors want to see demos and milestones on a quarterly rhythm. When the clock is ticking that loudly, 996 starts to feel like the default rather than a choice.

But I'd push back on one thing. Long hours and real progress are not the same. In robotics, a lot of the work is debugging physical systems, collecting data, waiting on hardware. You can't brute-force that with a twelfth hour of sitting at a desk. The people I've seen make breakthroughs usually had space to think, to run the experiment that looked like a waste of time. Teams that are exhausted tend to repeat yesterday's experiment with a slightly different hyperparameter.

So my read is that 996 is a symptom of competition, not a strategy for winning it. The pressure is genuine, but how a team responds to it is still a decision. The leaders I respect most protect their people's judgment, because in the end judgment is the scarce resource, not hours.

r001.rationale: It says teams fear being scooped or missing a window, but does not identify top members leaving for a leading team if their team falls behind.

r002.rationale: It links competitive pressure to long hours, but does not say teams intensify work to retain talent.

r003.rationale: It describes the field as moving quickly, but does not attribute recent progress to research effort increased by competition.

astra-6.text:
I think the pressure comes partly from uncertainty. In AI and robotics, things move quickly, and teams worry that if they slow down, someone else will reach an important milestone first. Working longer hours becomes a very visible way to respond to that fear. But visible effort isn’t necessarily useful progress.

In robotics, especially, you can’t solve every problem by spending more time at your desk. You need experiments, reliable hardware, and time to understand why something failed. If people are exhausted, they can make mistakes that actually slow the whole team down.

So I would distinguish urgency from a permanent 996 schedule. There are moments when a team needs an intense push toward a clear goal. But if that becomes the everyday expectation, it can undermine the creativity and judgment you’re competing on in the first place. The harder responsibility for leadership is deciding what matters, what to stop doing, and how to help people sustain good work.

r001.rationale: The response mentions fear that another team may reach a milestone first, but not that the strongest members might leave for the leading team.

r002.rationale: It does not say teams intensify work to retain talent.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute recent rapid progress in AI and robotics to research effort induced by competition.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the pressure comes from a sense that the field is moving so quickly that if you slow down, you’ll miss the opportunity. In AI and robotics, there’s always another model, another demonstration, another company making progress. That can create an arms race in working hours.

But I would distinguish urgency from effectiveness. Robotics depends on experiments, hardware reliability, and careful judgment. Working longer doesn’t automatically make those things happen faster, and fatigue can lead to mistakes that cost you more time later.

There will be periods when a team works intensely toward a milestone. The problem is when that becomes the permanent expectation—nine to nine, six days a week. I think the more useful question is whether you’re choosing the right problems, learning quickly from experiments, and building a team that can sustain its progress. Those are stronger competitive advantages than the number of hours people spend in the office.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that strong team members would leave for a leading team if their own team fell behind.

r002.rationale: It describes fear of missing out and an arms race in working hours, but does not identify retaining talent as the reason teams intensify work.

r003.rationale: It notes rapid progress in the field, but does not attribute that progress to increased research effort caused by competition.
